questions.scenario: A team's image is 1.1 GB and contains the JDK, Maven, the source code and the .git directory. Security review rejects it.
questions.question: Which change addresses the main problems?
options: Compress the image with gzip
A multi-stage build: compile in a JDK stage and copy only the extracted application layers into a slim JRE runtime stage, with a .dockerignore excluding .git, target and .env
Delete the .git folder at runtime
Use the latest tag of the JDK image
questions.explanation: Build tools and sources never need to ship. Multi-stage builds keep them in a throwaway stage, and .dockerignore keeps sensitive files out of the build context.

questions.scenario: Every small code change causes the CI image build to download all Maven dependencies again and push 120 MB to the registry.
questions.question: What improves caching?
options: Disable the Docker layer cache
Copy pom.xml and resolve dependencies before copying src, and copy Spring Boot's extracted layers (dependencies first, application last)
Add RUN apt-get update at the top of the Dockerfile
Combine all instructions into a single RUN
questions.explanation: Docker reuses cached layers until an input changes. Putting slow-changing inputs first means a code change rebuilds and pushes only the small application layer.

questions.scenario: A service runs in a container limited to 1 GB, started with -Xmx1g. It is regularly killed by the orchestrator with exit code 137.
questions.question: What is the likely cause and fix?
options: Heap plus non-heap memory exceeds the container limit; size the heap as a percentage (for example -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75) so other JVM memory fits
The JVM ignores container limits; upgrade Docker
The image is too large; use Alpine
Exit code 137 means the tests failed
questions.explanation: The JVM also uses metaspace, thread stacks, code cache and direct buffers. If the heap alone may use the entire limit, the container exceeds it and is OOM-killed (137).

questions.scenario: In Docker Compose, the app container starts before PostgreSQL accepts connections and crashes with 'connection refused'.
questions.question: What is the correct fix?
options: Add sleep 30 to the application's entrypoint
Give the postgres service a health check (pg_isready) and use depends_on with condition: service_healthy
Run PostgreSQL inside the application container
Use links instead of depends_on
questions.explanation: depends_on alone waits only for the container to start. A health-check condition waits until the database is actually ready.

questions.scenario: You are hardening the runtime image for a payments service.
questions.question: Which practices improve security? (Choose two.)
options: Scan the image in CI (for example Trivy) and fail on fixable critical vulnerabilities
Pass the database password as a Docker build argument
Tag and deploy images as latest
Run as a dedicated non-root user
questions.explanation: Non-root execution limits damage from a compromise, and scanning catches known vulnerabilities. Build arguments are visible in image history, and latest makes deployments non-reproducible.

questions.scenario: Inside Docker Compose, the app's datasource URL is jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/wallet and it cannot connect to the postgres service.
questions.question: Why?
options: Inside the app container, localhost is the app container itself; use the service name, jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/wallet
Port 5432 must be published to the host
Compose networks block JDBC
PostgreSQL does not support Docker
questions.explanation: Each container has its own network namespace. Compose provides DNS so services reach each other by service name.

questions.scenario: A platform team wants consistent, non-root, patchable images for 200 Spring Boot services without maintaining 200 Dockerfiles.
questions.question: Which approach fits?
options: Cloud Native Buildpacks via spring-boot:build-image (Paketo), with base images updated centrally
A single Dockerfile copied into every repository and edited by hand
Building images manually on a developer laptop
Running services directly on hosts without containers
questions.explanation: Buildpacks produce standardised, layered, non-root images with SBOMs, and base layers can be patched consistently across services.
